video_title: MacroVoices #556 Luke Gromen: US Midterms & Beyond
gist: Luke Gromen explains why the prolonged Hormuz closure hasn't yet crushed the economy (China/SPR drawdowns), argues Iran is winning a munitions war of attrition aimed at the US bond market, and flags an underappreciated risk: AI white-collar layoffs driving consumer defaults on $19T of debt, where each 5% equals ~40% of US bank equity. He sees recession Treasury supply of ~$5T+ that only the Fed can absorb, fades bond rallies, holds 30% cash/T-bills, and predicts AI-driven unrest from 2027; the market desk offers a COF bear put spread and technical reads on oil, gold, Mag 7 and the euro.

insights.claim: Luke Gromen's April 16 prediction that the Strait of Hormuz could stay closed until early July was ridiculed, yet the strait has stayed effectively closed for twice that long, though the feared economic damage has not yet materialized.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Gromen's geopolitical duration calls have been more right than consensus; the economic lag is the key open question.

insights.claim: Gromen says the economic impact was slower than expected because China constrained demand and drew down its SPR, and the US and other Western nations made coordinated SPR releases.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Buffers that delayed the shock are being depleted, raising risk of a later supply squeeze.
insights.quote: underestimated the degree to which China would constrain its demand and run down its SPR reserves

insights.claim: Gromen hears that in some emerging markets fertilizer is too expensive to order, so the food inflation shock may show up next year via lower crop yields rather than this year, making it initially bearish but ultimately very bullish for row crop prices.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Lagged yield hit implies 2027 food/grain upside despite near-term weakness.
insights.quote: ultimately very very bullish for prices for crop prices, row crop prices, initially it might actually be somewhat bearish

insights.claim: Erik Townsend argues refinery strikes in Russia, Saudi Arabia and Iran could reduce global refining capacity for years because refineries take 10 years to build, a risk he says the market is underpricing.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Persistent crack-spread blowouts and product tightness may outlast the war.
insights.quote: refineries take 10 years to build

insights.claim: Gromen notes crude is much higher than 6-8 months ago and diesel in parts of the world is approaching $200 a barrel despite SPR releases and offline refineries, and suggests China increasing purchases may be absorbing supply.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: China's restocking is a possible hidden demand source keeping crude elevated.
insights.quote: diesel prices in certain parts of the world are approaching $200 a barrel

insights.claim: Patrick Ceresna says oil only modestly responds to peace headlines and quickly regains highs, likely anticipating post-midterm re-escalation, with technical upside to the $120 prior high on WTI.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Oil remains in a decisive bull trend; peace headlines are fade-able.
insights.quote: a technical upside is back to the $120 previous highs on WTI

insights.claim: Gromen argues Iran doesn't need to beat the US militarily, only the bond market; when he said so on February 27 the 10-year was 3.94%, and it later hit 5.3%.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: War-driven fiscal and inflation pressure transmits through US yields.
insights.quote: Iran doesn't have to beat the US, it just has to beat the bond market

insights.claim: Gromen's framework: Iran forces the US to expend air defense missiles faster than it can replenish them (illustratively 150-300 used vs ~100 produced a month), eventually forcing the US to pull resources from other regions or fold.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Munitions production rates, and Chinese rare earth supply, are the binding constraint on US endurance.
insights.quote: The Americans burn 200 to 300 missiles a month, the Americans can only replace 100 missiles a month

insights.claim: Gromen says US bases have taken serious damage without adequate air defense, the US cannot invade without air superiority it hasn't lacked in 80 years, and Russia and China are happy to resupply Iran, so he expects the conflict to keep dragging on.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Expect prolonged conflict, ongoing energy risk, and political cost to the administration.
insights.quote: I think it's going to continue dragging on

themes.theme: Treasury market stress and fiscal dominance

insights.claim: Gromen flags that the 10-year Treasury yield fell as much as 20 bp intraday on a Thursday while gold fell $50, oil rose 3%, Bitcoin fell and the dollar rose, a correlation break he says he has seen only on catastrophic days like 9/11, Lehman and COVID in 31 years.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: An anomalous bond rally may signal informed positioning ahead of a risk-off event.
insights.quote: the 10-year fell as much as 20 basis points intraday

insights.claim: Gromen speculates the bond move may reflect someone getting a heads-up that a losing Trump administration would 'dump the board over' via Bessent's threatened fiscal consolidation between November 4 and January 3, 2027, noting the CFTC was reportedly told to stand down on investigating oil-market tip-offs.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Lame-duck fiscal tightening risk could tank stocks and commodities while bonds rally.

insights.claim: Gromen expects the Fed to either hold or hike 25 bp and says it doesn't matter much; the market desk later reports a hawkish hold from Warsh with little market reaction.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen / Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Fed policy is secondary to fiscal and geopolitical drivers.

insights.claim: Gromen says US interest plus entitlements plus Veterans Affairs already runs at 105% of receipts, and a recession would add 600-800 bp of GDP (about $1.8-2.4 trillion) to the roughly $2 trillion deficit.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Recession would roughly double deficits, overwhelming Treasury demand.
insights.quote: US interest plus the entitlements and plus Veterans Affairs is running at 105% of receipts

insights.claim: Gromen tallies recession Treasury supply at roughly $5.1-5.2 trillion counting ~$4 trillion deficits, $200-300 billion of bank selling, ~$600 billion of foreign central bank selling since February, and hedge fund de-grossing (hedge funds own 8% of the market), concluding the Fed is the only buyer.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Recession leads to Fed debt monetization, whatever it is called.
insights.quote: there's only one buyer. It's the Fed.

insights.claim: Gromen would fade any bond rally triggered by an AI slowdown because Bessent's quarterly refunding would reveal issuance closer to $3.5 trillion than $2 trillion, unless the Fed, Treasury buybacks or a shift to bills intervene.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Trade view: fade long-end rallies absent explicit Fed/Treasury support.
insights.quote: I would fade the bond rally all day long

insights.claim: Gromen holds 30% of his liquid net worth in cash and T-bills, preferring caution over shorting because fiscal dominance means liquidity gets supplied whenever the Treasury market acts up.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Even bears avoid outright shorts in a fiscal-dominance regime.
insights.quote: I'm sitting in 30% of my liquid net worth in cash and T-bills

themes.theme: AI job loss as consumer credit risk

insights.claim: Gromen's underappreciated second-derivative risk: with $19 trillion in US consumer debt, every 5% AI-driven default (about $1 trillion) equals roughly 40% of the $2.6 trillion US bank equity capital base.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: AI white-collar displacement could become a banking-system capital event, not just a labor story.
insights.quote: every 5% default rate increase on consumer debt as a result of AI unemployment or deflation in wages is equal to 40% 40% of the total equity base

insights.claim: Gromen cites recent AI-linked layoffs: Kroger reportedly ~37% of corporate workforce, American Express and Barclays 5% each, and Microsoft buying out 27% of its workforce, calling Microsoft the 'we're going to need a bigger boat' moment.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Corporate AI layoffs are accelerating and undermine the 'jobs will be fine' camp.
insights.quote: we're going to need a bigger boat moment

insights.claim: Gromen says banks facing AI-driven credit losses could only cut lending, sell Treasuries, issue equity, or slow the economy, all of which are bad for risk assets and the US debt position.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Bank deleveraging would add to Treasury supply and tighten credit.

insights.claim: Gromen notes bank stocks, consumer credit names, Blackstone, Blue Owl, American Express and Capital One have massively underperformed the S&P over three to six months, asking why own them if AI works.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Market may already be pricing AI-driven consumer credit deterioration.
insights.quote: If AI works, why would I want to own any of this stuff?

insights.claim: Patrick Ceresna's trade: with Capital One (COF) around $204.88, a January 15, 2027 200/175 bear put spread for about $5.96 debit offers max profit of $19.04 (~3:1), or the January 200 put outright at $7.95 given implied vol near one-year lows.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Defined-risk way to express AI-driven consumer credit deterioration.
insights.quote: I'm looking at the January 15th, 2027 200 by 175 bear put spread trading around $5.96 net debit

themes.theme: AI capex, bailouts and political fallout

insights.claim: Gromen says the administration banning DeepSeek (transcribed 'Deep Seek') from government programs contradicts David Sacks' no-regulation stance and effectively builds a moat around OpenAI and Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Policy is protecting incumbent US AI labs.
insights.quote: That's a moat that they helped try to put up around the economics of OpenAI and Anthropic.

insights.claim: Gromen hears credible rumblings that contingency plans for stepping in if AI credit financing breaks were discussed in Washington over a year ago, as AI is now too big to fail.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Expect a policy backstop for AI capex in a bust scenario.
insights.quote: AI's now too big to fail.

insights.claim: Townsend likens the AI credit-driven buildout to the 2000 dot-com bust and argues a bust could let China, about 6 months behind per Matt Berry, take AI leadership, making a bailout a national security argument for Bessent.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: National-security framing raises odds of government support for AI spending.

insights.claim: Townsend highlights that Anthropic's S-1 risk factors state that advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, which he says is likely unprecedented in an SEC filing and could give Democrats ammunition against AI bailouts.
insights.speaker: Erik Townsend
insights.so_what: Disclosure language could shape political battles over AI support.
insights.quote: pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity

insights.claim: Gromen predicts that if AI succeeds and is propped up, rapid white-collar job loss in a heterogeneous, growing US population will drive accelerating political instability and civil unrest starting in 2027, citing Peter Turchin on elite overproduction.
insights.speaker: Luke Gromen
insights.so_what: Social unrest is a second-order tail risk of AI success.
insights.quote: It'll start to get litigated in 2027

insights.claim: Ceresna notes Microsoft's quarterly free cash flow of about $18 billion versus Alphabet's minus $9 billion, highlighting a split between funding the AI build-out and delivering returns; Alphabet gapped down into a clear downtrend.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: AI capex winners vs. losers increasingly judged on free cash flow.
insights.quote: Microsoft's quarterly free cash flow was like 18 billion dollars versus Alphabet minus 9 billion

insights.claim: Ceresna says the Nasdaq is below its 50-day moving average in a bear flag, the S&P 500 is holding above systematic sell zones around 7,600-7,700, and the Mag 7 make up 35% of the S&P 500.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: A break below 7,600-7,700 could trigger CTA and vol-target deleveraging.

insights.claim: Ceresna says gold is sitting on $4,000 support with a distributive chart and no buyers, risking a further 5-10% drawdown, though he remains long-term bullish.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Near-term gold downside risk despite a bullish secular view.
insights.quote: gold remains at a risk of a breakdown

insights.claim: Ceresna says the euro is near 52-week lows and a break of 1.11 could drive further dollar strength, keeping the dollar bull trend intact.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Euro weakness is the swing factor for the dollar index.

insights.claim: Ceresna flags uranium spot around $91 holding above $90 while uranium equities are in a decisive downtrend dragged down by AI selling, a possible buying opportunity, and notes Brazil's EWZ gapped down 20-30% after Bolsonaro unexpectedly lost.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Uranium equity/spot divergence may offer an entry point.

insights.claim: Ceresna says the USDA raised its corn production forecast and large speculators sold roughly 166,000 net contracts over two weeks, washing out a crowded bullish ag trade; copper is neutral with a break below 650 risking a squeeze-out.
insights.speaker: Patrick Ceresna
insights.so_what: Crowded commodity longs are being liquidated.
